intros.market: Five CAs control 93.7% of the public web certificate market. The Internet Security Research Group leads at 41.1%, followed by Google Trust Services (15.1%), DigiCert (13.9%), GoDaddy (12.9%), and Sectigo (10.7%). The remaining 80 CAs share just 6.3% of issuance despite holding equal trust store access, creating a systemic dependency on a handful of operators whose failure would cascade across the internet.
intros.trust: 335 roots are trusted across the four major browser stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four and just 38 CA owners hold universal trust. Microsoft's store contains 142 roots not trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating operational fragmentation where certificate chains valid in Edge fail in other browsers. This disagreement reflects divergent oversight models and forces CAs to maintain parallel hierarchies, multiplying the attack surface while complicating incident response coordination.
intros.conc: The market HHI of 2412 sits in the moderately concentrated range, but the top three CAs alone control 70% of issuance (CR3). Chrome and Safari together represent 94.6% of browser usage, amplifying the impact of any failure at ISRG, Google, or DigiCert. This concentration creates single points of systemic failure where a CA compromise or distrust event could instantly affect hundreds of millions of sites.
intros.tail: 80 CAs in the trust store tail collectively issue just 6.3% of certificates, yet each holds the same browser trust as the top five. Many operate below meaningful audit scrutiny and lack the operational maturity of high-volume CAs, as evidenced by 54 CAs appearing in the 1,464-incident corpus. Low issuance volume correlates with reduced root program oversight attention, creating disproportionate risk per certificate issued.
intros.geo: US-incorporated CAs issue 88.9% of all certificates despite representing only 16 of 95 trusted CAs. European CAs account for 48 organizations but just 11.05% of issuance, while 17 Asia-Pacific CAs collectively issue 0.05%. This geographic concentration creates regulatory jurisdiction risk and positions US legal frameworks as de facto global policy, with GDPR-region CAs largely marginalized despite local compliance advantages.
intros.gov: 31 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store inclusion but collectively issue only 0.06% of certificates. These entities span high-risk jurisdictions including China, Russia, and several Middle Eastern states, creating surveillance and interception risks disproportionate to their issuance volume. Their trust store presence enables man-in-the-middle attacks within their territories regardless of market share, as seen in historical incidents involving CNNIC and Kazakhstan.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk for compelled certificate issuance or surveillance abuse: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk. These classifications reflect laws enabling state access to private keys, gag orders preventing disclosure, or demonstrated willingness to weaponize PKI for censorship. The 88.9% US concentration creates a separate risk surface under FISA and national security letter frameworks.
intros.ops: 1,464 incidents across 54 CAs break down into misissuance (581), governance failures (451), revocation problems (310), and validation errors (122). Only 23% of incidents are self-detected by CAs, with external researchers (19%), automated tools (18%), and audits (8%) finding the majority. 168 incidents involved policy violations and 118 involved disclosure failures, indicating systemic gaps in both controls and transparency even among high-volume operators.
intros.crypto: Root algorithm and key size data reveal ongoing exposure to deprecated cryptography and non-compliant standards. The expanding regulatory surface creates a moving target where CAs must simultaneously maintain legacy roots for compatibility while deploying quantum-resistant algorithms. The 47-day validity floor arriving in 2029 will force cryptographic agility that many CAs have not demonstrated in their incident histories.
intros.distrust: 16 total distrust events show a pattern of compliance and operational failures rather than cryptographic compromises. 10 events involved patterns of repeated issues, 14 involved compliance or operational failures, and the posture distribution skews toward negligent noncompliance (7) and demonstrated incompetence (3). The median runway of 1,185 days from incident disclosure to distrust reflects root programs' reluctance to act decisively, allowing prolonged risk exposure before removal.
intros.policy: Among 42 active TLS issuers, only 12 are ready for the March 2029 47-day validity limit based on actual certificate replacement behavior. 4 CAs remain at risk of missing even the March 2026 200-day threshold, and 5 face risk at the March 2027 100-day step. This readiness gap exists partly because the regulatory surface has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,651 total obligations, with 76% classified as mandatory. The compliance complexity increases faster than CA operational maturity, as evidenced by zero new ballots since 2022 despite this expansion.
intros.governance: Root program oversight covered only 18.4% of Chrome incidents, 9.9% of Mozilla incidents, and 5.4% of Apple incidents in 2025, down from 67.8% and 78% in 2019 for Chrome and Mozilla respectively. Microsoft provided zero substantive oversight across all 223 incidents. Chrome has commented on 290 substantive bugs lifetime and Mozilla on 248, but recent engagement (109 and 46 bugs respectively) has not kept pace with incident growth, creating a surveillance gap where CAs operate with declining accountability.
intros.community: 56 organizations are CA/Browser Forum members but only 21 actively contribute, leaving 35 with zero ballot participation. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo has proposed 36 ballots and Sectigo leads organizational contribution, but the silent majority of CAs consume policy without shaping it. This participation gap means high-volume operators in the market tab effectively write rules for the 80-CA tail that lacks voice or technical engagement in standards development.
intros.audit: Auditors detected only 26% of the 415 in-scope incidents that occurred during their audit periods, despite issuing letters for 88 CAs. 38 CAs show high transparency gaps between clean audit opinions and documented Bugzilla incident histories, and 6 CAs received qualified opinions. Only 1 CA has adopted ETSI EN 319 411-1 v3.5, and 57.2% of WebTrust findings and 62.7% of ETSI findings are self-reported rather than auditor-discovered. 20 CAs changed auditors in 2025, suggesting dissatisfaction or opinion shopping, while auditor concentration (HHI 486.2) remains low enough that CAs can migrate to more permissive firms.
